# Creating {#sec-creating}

In the data lifecycle, the "Create" stage covers every route by which a new dataset comes into existence, including simulation, remote sensing, and assembling new datasets from existing sources. For most ecologists, though, data creation begins with collecting observations in the field or lab and digitising them to produce a raw dataset, and that is the focus of this chapter. If you are assembling a new dataset from existing sources, much of the same planning and preparation applies, with one important addition: you must record the source of each piece of data so that the link to the original is never lost (see @sec-reusing). Whatever form your data creation takes, planning how you will do it before you start will save considerable time and frustration later.

## Planning to collect your data

Effective and smooth data collection involves detailed planning, such as identifying necessary variables of interest and choosing an appropriate data collection method. Developing a robust plan for data collection prior to undertaking data collection activities will improve the ease of subsequent collection and organisation of your data (see @sec-planning).

## Key things to consider prior to data collection:

- What data will you collect?
- How will you collect these data?
- How much time do you have to collect and collate your data?
- How much data do you need to achieve the goals of your study?
- Are there administrative hurdles that need to be cleared within/outside of your institution prior to planning field or lab visits? For example risk assessments and ethics approvals.
- Have you factored in enough time and resources to conduct a pilot test?
- What examples of data collection for your target data exist in the literature?
- What structure did these data take, and how is this different from the way you will structure your data, if at all?
- What are the key data collection lessons learned in these previous examples?

Considering these aspects allows researchers to create a data collection protocol, or a best practice guide on how the desired data will be collected. A strong data collection protocol will ensure high-quality data are collected with limited setbacks. Protocols should be carefully documented and edited as required once data collection begins and additional issues are identified. Excellent examples of how to prepare a robust data collection protocol are detailed by Jones, Spence-Jones, and Greiser (2026)[^creating-1].

[^creating-1]: Jones, F. A. M., Spence-Jones, H. C., & Greiser, C. (2026). A short guide for effective field data collection. Methods in Ecology and Evolution, 17, 1042–1050. https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210x.70259.

## Data collection

Proper quality control during data collection is important because planned data collection activities are time and resource limited, often representing a singular opportunity to collect data from a given situation, e.g. on a particular day in the field. Researchers should be critical of methods before data collection begins because high-quality methods are more likely to result in high-quality data. Likewise, when data collection is underway, detailed documentation of the collection process should be kept as an integral part of quality assurance and added to the data collection protocol.

**Adequate preparation**. Any good data collection process begins with strong preparation. Researchers should refer back to the steps taken to clear administrative hurdles (such as ethics approvals and risk assessments) to prepare for potential issues in the data collection process. Researchers should have a detailed geographical understanding of the locations they will collect samples from before any data are collected, and a collection template should be developed to ensure that all information is collected consistently, especially if there are multiple collectors. Researchers may also consider widening the possible applications of data, and therefore increase their impact, by adding additional variables and parameters to data, e.g. wider landscape variables, which will encourage reuse and potentially open up new avenues for research. Although preparation is particularly key for fieldwork, especially if time in the field is limited, these points equally apply to working in the lab, and even to working on a computer. Preparation saves time.

**Data collection in practice**. Researchers should ensure that all necessary equipment or instruments have been properly calibrated and that quality checks have been undertaken prior to entering the field/lab. Once data collection activities have begun, detailed notes should be taken in an agreed and easily readable format. This will aid other researchers to understand the process taken, conditions that will affect the quality of data collected, any issues encountered, protocols breached, or any issues envisioned in future data collection activities. Remember to record the precision and accuracy for any measurement. For example, certain measurements will be taken to the nearest mm, others might be to the nearest metre. This detail will be important when you get to your data analysis. Precision is how repeatable the measurement is, accuracy is how close the measurement is to the true value.

**Care**. Before going into the field all researchers should have adequate training, and clear expectations for data collection, health and safety, and behaviour should be set. See the [BES Inclusive Fieldwork](https://www.britishecologicalsociety.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/BES-Inclusive-fieldwork-guide.pdf) guide for more details. This is particularly important in the field, but also applies in the lab or at a computer.

**Backups**. Back up collected data as soon as practically possible, and keep multiple copies in different locations (see @sec-preserving for a full discussion of backup strategy). Ideally, if data collection is in handwritten format, photographs of datasheets should be taken and uploaded immediately to avoid the loss of data. This practice is best done at the end of each day, if time allows. When uploading data with sensitive information, ensure that only authorised team members can access the files.

::: callout-tip
### Community (citizen) science data

Community science (previously known as citizen science) is the involvement of volunteers in research data collection. Community science has a long history, especially in biological recording, and volunteer data collection is increasingly vital for expanding scientific knowledge where researchers have limited time and resources. Some community science projects are highly structured with fixed protocols, trained volunteers and regular data collection effort. Others are less structured and involve volunteers entering records into sites like [iNaturalist](https://www.inaturalist.org/), [iRecord](https://irecord.org.uk/) and [eBird](https://ebird.org/home), whenever they choose. While the data and insights acquired from such projects is extensive, these data have unique issues related to data quality and bias, which should be considered when using them. For example, community scientists are more likely to collect data in easily accessible areas, and common/easily identified species are more likely to be recorded than rare ones. Some suggestions for how we can deal with these issues can be found in Johnson et al 2023[^creating-2]. These considerations should be factored into all stages of the data lifecycle when using community science data. It is also important to carefully think about how you will share data collected by volunteers, and how you will ensure their input is appropriately credited and rewarded.
:::

[^creating-2]: Johnston, A., Matechou, E. & Dennis, E. B. (2023). Outstanding challenges and future directions for biodiversity monitoring using citizen science data. Methods in Ecology and Evolution, 14, 103–116. https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.13834.

## Data digitisation

Once data has been collected, a detailed digitisation plan should be followed. Data may already be in digital format which feeds directly into a computer, or they may have been collected as hand-written notes. Either way, some level of data processing will be involved to produce the digital raw dataset, which can eventually be used for data analysis (see @sec-processing). Ideally, data digitisation should take place shortly after the completion of data collection, when the data are still fresh in the researcher’s memory. This will make transferring the data into a raw dataset quicker and more accurate than waiting some time before doing this. There are several key aspects to consider during the digitisation stage. All of these aspects should be part of your planning process (see @sec-planning).

**Data structure**. An adequate database structure for the raw data should be chosen which organises the data and data files. All data files should use a consistent format e.g. one row represents a complete record and each column represents all parameters that make up that record (known as spreadsheet format). Each entry should refer solely to one piece of data. Plain text characters should be used to ensure data are neat and readable by a maximum number of software or programmes (e.g. ASCII, Unicode). Using unique informative identifiers (IDs) will be useful in the event of lost field labels, or missing information. These IDs may follow a logical structure which indicates the time and place an observation was taken, such as ‘Site1_PlotA_Reading1’. Avoid special characters and values beginning with zeroes when recording digital data, as this can lead to misreading your data in some programmes, and make checking the data in .csv format later confusing.

**Data storage**. Once a raw dataset has been accurately created, the raw values should not be amended directly. All calculations or cross referencing should be done in the chosen data analysis programme (see @sec-processing). File names for raw datasets should indicate the exact nature of the data to avoid later confusion when reading data into data analysis programmes, e.g. ‘Plantdata_Highlands_Jun26.csv’.

::: callout-tip
### Beware of spreadsheets and auto-correct!

Spreadsheet software, such as Microsoft Excel, can silently convert data entries into dates, numbers, or other formats. For example, gene symbols such as SEPT1 and MARCH1 are automatically reformatted as calendar dates, while identifiers like "2/3" become fractions. This is not a minor nuisance: Ziemann et al. (2016)[^creating-3] found that roughly one in five published genomics papers contained gene name errors introduced by Microsoft Excel. The problem was so pervasive that in 2020 the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee actually renamed several human genes to avoid the issue (e.g. SEPT1 became SEPTIN1, MARCH1 became MARCHF1). To avoid this format cells as "Text" before entering data, or better still, use a plain-text format such as .csv with a dedicated text editor or scripting environment for data entry. If you use Excel, check your data after saving as autocorrection errors are often introduced silently on save or reopen. Exporting can also introduce errors, so always make sure to carefully check your data!
:::

[^creating-3]: Ziemann, M., Eren, Y. & El-Osta, A. Gene name errors are widespread in the scientific literature. Genome Biol 17, 177 (2016). https://doi.org/10.1186/s13059-016-1044-7.

::: border
### Creating checklist

- [ ] Are all administrative requirements completed before planning data collection, e.g. ethics approval, risk assessment?
- [ ] Have you agreed upon a robust data collection protocol that takes into consideration the specific place and time where you will be collecting your data?
- [ ] Have you developed a collection template for all researchers conducting data collection?
- [ ] Have you set up a secure online folder to store backups of collected data?
- [ ] Are there any critical issues that were noted during data collection that need to be addressed before collating your data into a raw dataset? If yes, have you dealt with these?
- [ ] Have you decided on a format for your raw dataset?
- [ ] Have you assigned unique IDs to each observation, avoiding any special characters in the IDs?
- [ ] Have you created backups of your raw dataset?
:::
